newsitem.title: CANADA: Canada panel rules against homosexual on pensions.
newsitem.headline: Canada panel rules against homosexual on pensions.

text.p: The Canadian Human Rights Tribunal ruled on Friday that companies do not have to give pension benefits to partners of homosexual employees.
But the court urged the federal government to change the law so pensions could be granted in the same way that other benefits such as medical plans are for homosexual spouses.
The case involved a customer sales and service agent, Niels Laessoe, who had pressed Air Canada to agree to give pension benefits to his partner, Ronald Sowden, in the event Laessoe died.
"The employer is justified in not extending pension benefits to same-sex spouses when it is prohibited from doing so in equal fashion by the provisions of federal legislation," the tribunal ruled.

Noting that pensions are governed by federal law, it said: "We urge the federal government to act swiftly to amend the legislation that prevents employers such as Air Canada from extending pension benefits to same-sex spouses."
The homosexual rights lobbying group Egale said it was clear that the federal government was discriminating against homosexuals by maintaining its current laws.

"We will make sure that the federal government hears that message loud and clear," Egale Executive Director John Fisher told a news conference in Toronto. "We will keep working to make sure that they do change the Income Tax Act, and if necessary we will keep fighting this through the courts."
The conservative Evangelical Fellowship of Canada said it was important for such questions to be decided by legislatures, more accountable to citizens than courts.

"We believe very strongly in the (heterosexual) marriage relationship, and it should have some kind of preferred status in the law, because it has shown to be the best relationship for the stability of families," the group's Social Action Committee Chairwoman Janet Buckingham said.
